intro: Move a tax up or down — Smith County’s or Tyler’s property tax rate, or a sales tax — and see what it does to a household’s bill, to each budget, and to what that money could pay for or would have to give up. Every rate and tax base comes from a cited document.

household.homestead_label: It’s my homestead (takes off the $140,000 school exemption)
household.where: The household example is a home inside Tyler city limits, Tyler ISD, and the Tyler Junior College district, so it pays all four property taxes and both sales taxes. All four 2026 rates are from the county tax office’s Truth-in-Taxation database.
household.note: Texas taxes property on its full appraised value, in cents per $100. The default home is Tyler’s median-valued homestead for 2026 ($240,428, from the city’s taxpayer impact statement). The homestead box takes off the state’s $140,000 school exemption (Tax Code §11.13(b)); county, city, and college homestead exemptions aren’t confirmed yet and aren’t subtracted, and over-65 exemptions and tax ceilings aren’t modeled. Taxable purchases are your own guess; most groceries aren’t taxed in Texas.

layers.name: Smith County tax rate
layers.base_note: Each 1¢ per $100 raises about $2,932,847 a year — the county’s own budget math (General Fund taxes $77,754,758 on 26.5117¢). The 37.4088¢ is 31.7617¢ for operations and 5.6471¢ for debt.

caps.text: This is above the county's FY27 voter-approval rate of 39.2898¢. In most cases a rate above it triggers an automatic election.

layers.name: City of Tyler tax rate
layers.base_note: Each 1¢ per $100 raises about $1,397,484 a year: the city’s General Fund expects $33,827,912 in property tax at 24.2063¢.

caps.text: Tyler's 2026 rate is already at its voter-approval rate of 24.2063¢. Going higher would send the rate to the voters in most cases.

layers.name: Tyler ISD tax rate
layers.base_note: Each 1¢ per $100 raises about $1,313,720 a year on the district’s $13,137,201,946 of 2026 taxable value (Form 50-859, line 21). The board cut the rate from 84.5¢ to 83.5¢ for 2026.

caps.text: This is above Tyler ISD's 2026 voter-approval rate of 84.7024¢. A school district above it needs voters to approve the rate at an election.

layers.name: Tyler Junior College tax rate
layers.base_note: Each 1¢ per $100 raises about $2,069,423 a year on the college district’s $20,694,229,152 of 2026 taxable value (Form 50-856, line 22). The rate rose from 18.5068¢ in 2025 to 21.0312¢ — its voter-approval rate, the most it could set without an election.

caps.text: TJC's 2026 rate is already at its voter-approval rate of 21.0312¢. Going higher would send the rate to the voters in most cases.

layers.name: Smith County sales tax
layers.base_note: Each 1% would raise about $60 million a year: the county’s half-cent brings its General Fund about $30,000,000 (FY27). By state rule this half-cent exists to lower property taxes — the county’s rate worksheet counts it as replacing about 11.8¢ per $100.

source.page: revenue detail p. 30; rate worksheet line 41

caps.text: Inside Tyler the local sales tax is already 2% (1.5% city + 0.5% county). A county can't raise its tax if the combined local rate would "exceed two percent at any location in the county."

layers.name: City of Tyler sales tax
layers.base_note: Tyler’s 1.5% is 1% for the General Fund plus the voter-approved half-cent run by a separate corporation. Each 1% raises roughly $45 million: the General Fund expects $45,175,855 in sales and use taxes in FY27.

caps.text: Tyler's combined local sales tax is already 2%. A city can't raise its tax if the combined local rate would "exceed two percent at any location in the municipality."

law.text: Smith County's FY27 rate is 37.4088¢ per $100. Its no-new-revenue rate — the rate that would raise the same money as last year from the same property — is 35.764¢, and its voter-approval rate is 39.2898¢. Above the voter-approval rate, voters decide in most cases.

2026 adopted rates for a home in Tyler, per $100: Smith County 37.4088¢, City of Tyler 24.2063¢, Tyler ISD 83.5¢, Tyler Junior College 21.0312¢ — $1.661463 in all. Tyler and TJC adopted exactly their voter-approval rates; Tyler ISD cut its rate a penny.
Every Texas homestead gets a $140,000 exemption from school district taxes, and $60,000 more if the owner is 65 or older or disabled.
The voter-approval rate lets operating taxes grow at most 3.5% a year on the same property, plus what debt payments require.
Texas caps combined local sales tax at 2% at any location (state 6.25% + local 2% = 8.25%). Tyler is at the cap, so neither the county nor the city can raise sales tax there.
Smith County's half-cent is the kind voters adopt "to reduce the county property tax rate" — the county's rate worksheet counts it as replacing about 11.8¢ per $100.

Counties may grant a homestead exemption of up to 20% of value, and may freeze county taxes for over-65 and disabled homeowners (Tax Code §§11.13(n), 11.261). Smith County's current exemption amounts aren't confirmed here yet.

limits: Tax bases are held at this year’s values. Appraisals rise and fall, and Texas truth-in-taxation math resets the no-new-revenue and voter-approval rates every year.
A sales-tax change can change where people shop. This page assumes the same spending.
Smith County’s rate applies across the whole county, not just Tyler; Tyler’s rate applies only inside the city.
Only the $140,000 school homestead exemption is modeled. Over-65 and disability exemptions, local optional exemptions, and tax ceilings are not.
Tyler ISD’s taxable value already excludes homesteads frozen under the over-65 ceiling, so its per-cent figure is on the low side.
Paying bonds off early is only possible when the bonds allow it (their call dates).
Saving-up times ignore interest earned and rising construction costs.
